summary: Bonavista Bay light lit 1 October 1888 on Little Denier Island off Salvage: a 7.6 m prefabricated cast-iron tower, unattended since 1931 and still standing.

structures.note: Prefabricated iron tower, painted red and white; ordered from Victoria Works (Lighthouse Friends; heritage statement 89-201).
Lighthouse Friends describes the mansard-roofed keeper's dwelling; the heritage statement describes the tower and its setting only.

access.note: Grounds and tower closed (Lighthouse Friends); open status closed (Chance Heritage Trust).

events.note: Inspector Nevill's inspection: landing made, plans begun; no light built as a result
Nevill chooses Little Denier over King's Cove Head; road and store built to the summit
Lighthouse and keeper's dwelling built under J.T. Nevill's direction; construction 14 weeks
Light put into operation on 1 October 1888; revolving six-sided lens, white flash every 30 seconds
Robert Oakley, previously assistant keeper on Cabot Island, placed in charge
Light source changed to acetylene; range reduced from nineteen to ten miles (Lighthouse Friends)
Changed from a flash every 30 seconds to 7 s white and 3 s eclipse; source probably kerosene (Lighthouse Friends)
Light returned to acetylene and made unattended; gas cylinders changed about four times a year by tenders
Classified a Recognized Federal Heritage Building

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends gives 48.684722 N, 53.573333 W (53 34 24 W). The Coast Guard list gives 48 41 05.0 N, 053 35 24.0 W, and the Chance Heritage Trust gives 48.6856, -53.5899, which agree with the Coast Guard. The record's point is the Coast Guard point. The two points are about 1.2 km apart, not the more than 500 m in the record's note.

notes_for_editor: Characteristic conflict, not resolved: Lighthouse Friends and the Chance Heritage Trust say the light is solar powered and flashes once every three seconds; the Coast Guard list gives LFl W 6s (long flash every six seconds). The record keeps the Coast Guard value. Confirm with the Coast Guard before publishing a characteristic. The 1882 and 1887 inspections, the 1889 report and the 1888 construction details come from Lighthouse Friends, which cites the Journal of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland. That journal was not read; it is the primary source to check. The heritage statement adds the 1888 date, Nevill's direction and the 26-lighthouse claim. The 'only remaining examples' claim is the heritage statement's own wording ('thought to be'); the Chance Heritage Trust repeats it as a 'sole survivor' claim, which the story does not use. Keeper names are Lighthouse Friends' list, plus the 1894 directory. McAlpine's 1894-97 directory is a volunteer transcription; check against the page image before relying on Samuel Oakley. The story does not assume a relation between Robert and Samuel Oakley. Spelling: Lighthouse Friends says Cornick, Chance Heritage Trust says Conwick; the story uses Cornick (LF) with the variant noted. No storms, wrecks or rescues are sourced for this light, so that chapter is omitted. Newfoundland's own colonial reports and the Newfoundland press were not searched; the Canadian Marine reports in the corpus do not cover the colonial lights before 1949. Living-person rule: James Brown and the Hunter family are named only as Lighthouse Friends gives them, with no further detail. Check of this pass: the McAlpine transcription page says its entries are as they appear in the 1894 directory, though its title reads 1894-97; the story now says 1894. The Chance Heritage Trust page gives the light as flashing once every 3 seconds, which agrees with LF; the Coast Guard list marks the light seasonal. The story says so. The Chance page also repeats the 'sole survivor' claim; the story keeps the heritage statement's own 'thought to be' wording.
